The screen result can flip only if sponsorRecipient is a code-less address that later becomes a factory clone (the CREATE address keccak(rlp(factory, nonce)), via OZ Clones.clone). Sponsor purchases cannot be told apart from sybil buyers, so no single code operation removes the root cause. Partial fix: cap sponsorProceeds at reserveEntries×ENTRY_PRICE×95% and send the surplus to the winner/cash pool. That removes variant A; variant B would still need disclosure.

fields.smell: In NftWon, _settleWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:543-544, :554-555) makes 95% sponsorProceeds and 5% protocolFees releasable right away through releaseSponsorProceeds (:375-382) and releaseProtocolFees (:385-392). Neither depends on the winner's prize transfer in redeemWinningTicket (:329-337: prizeToken.transferFrom plus an ownerOf check) ever succeeding. DESIGN.md says prize contracts are untrusted. Suppose the prize contract stops honouring the clone's transfer after settlement, for example through a collection-admin pause, an ERC721C-style transfer-validator policy raised after deposit, or an upgradeable collection the sponsor controls. Then every redemption reverts. The winning ticket has no fallback claim: no conversion to CashWon, no refund, no timeout. The NFT is stranded in the clone after 100% of the pot has left.
fields.unverified: The trust model conflicts. IRaffle.sol:14-15 says supported prizes are honest, standards-compliant ERC-721s, while DESIGN.md calls prize contracts untrusted. A fully malicious prize is economically just a worthless prize, which no escrow can protect against, so real impact depends on the case where a third party freezes the collection. DESIGN.md also requires sponsor and treasury to claim independently after settlement, so holding proceeds until delivery would conflict with the spec. Sibling: receipt-type prizes whose value a third party can drain while escrowed (e.g. cancelable stream NFTs) have the same decoupled payout.
fields.description: NftWon pays the whole pot to sponsor and treasury whether or not the escrowed NFT can still be delivered, so if the prize contract later freezes the transfer, the winning ticket is left with a claim it cannot redeem and no cash or refund fallback.

fields.smell: _update (Raffle.sol:497-502) only screens destinations, so tickets can still move during Drawing: after requestDraw (:252) and before fulfillRandomWords (:509-524) records the result. winningEntry = randomWords[0] % totalEntries + 1 (:518) follows deterministically from the VRF proof in the pending Chainlink fulfillment transaction. A mempool observer can therefore know the winning ticket before the callback is included and act ahead of it: (a) fill standing collection-wide offers with tickets known to lose, or (b) buy the winning ticket from a pending listing. Chainlink's VRF guidance is to stop accepting inputs once randomness has been requested.
fields.unverified: The VRF v2.5 coordinator is not vendored in node_modules, so I did not verify how the word is derived from the proof or whether fulfillments pass through the public mempool. Transferability in every state is an explicit design choice (Raffle.sol:25-29 NatSpec, DESIGN.md). Only secondary-market counterparties trading during Drawing can be hurt.
fields.description: Tickets stay transferable while the draw outcome can be worked out publicly from the pending VRF fulfillment, so informed holders can offload losing tickets or snipe the winning ticket from counterparties who don't know the result.

fields.root_cause: Raffle.sol:544 (`sponsorAmount = grossPot - protocolFee`, with grossPot = unsettledPot at :539, credited at :554) pays the sponsor 95% of the whole pot, including entries the sponsor bought through any address. `buyEntries` (Raffle.sol:215-233) has no entry cap once `reserveEntries` is met and does not exclude the rebated party. Each sponsor-funded entry therefore costs the sponsor only 5% of ENTRY_PRICE but carries full weight in the uniform draw (Raffle.sol:518). This breaks DESIGN.md's uniform "one entry costs 1,000,000 units" for exactly one cohort. Earlier buyers cannot exit after the sponsor's late purchase: refunds open only at endTime+2d (Raffle.sol:286-287), and anyone, including the sponsor, can draw at endTime (Raffle.sol:242).
fields.internal_pre: The raffle resolves NftWon (totalEntries >= reserveEntries, Raffle.sol:521). The sponsor controls or colludes with sponsorRecipient, which is the default setup. The attack pays off whenever the NFT value V > 0.05 * organic entries N.
fields.external_pre: The sponsor has k USDC available from the last block before endTime until releaseSponsorProceeds, typically minutes: requestDraw at endTime, then 30 confirmations, then settle and release. 95% of it comes back. A flash loan does not work because entries lock funds across transactions.
fields.impact: The cohort of organic ticket holders who bought before the sale closed is left holding the loss.
fields.mitigation: Stop the sale at the reserve in buyEntries (`if (lastEntry > reserveEntries) revert ...`), so no sponsor-rebated entries can be minted after organic demand meets the reserve. A buyer blocklist on sponsor/sponsorRecipient alone is not enough, because purchases are permissionless (sybil). A sponsor fill of the gap below the reserve remains possible; it is tracked as a separate lead.

path:
  1. Sponsor S calls RaffleFactory.createRaffle for an NFT worth 10,000 USDC with reserveEntries = 5,000, sponsorRecipient = S, endTime = T.
  2. Alice calls buyEntries(alice, 10,000) and pays 10,000 USDC. Ticket #1 = [1, 10,000], unsettledPot = 10,000e6, and the reserve is met. Honest outcome: Alice wins the NFT with probability 1 and S nets 9,500 USDC.
  3. In the last block before T (timestamp T-12), S's fresh address S' calls buyEntries(S', 90,000) and pays 90,000 USDC. Ticket #2 = [10,001, 100,000]; totalEntries = 100,000; unsettledPot = 100,000e6. Nothing blocks it: Raffle.sol:215-221 checks only status, time, recipient and count.
  4. At T, S calls requestDraw. The VRF callback sets winningEntry uniform on [1, 100,000] and status = NftWon (Raffle.sol:518-521).
  5. settleWinningTicket sets protocolFees = 5,000 USDC and sponsorProceeds = 95,000 USDC (Raffle.sol:540, 544, 554). releaseSponsorProceeds then pays S 95,000, so S's net cash = 95,000 - 90,000 = +5,000 USDC.
  6. With probability 0.9, ticket #2 holds winningEntry, and S' calls redeemWinningTicket(2) to take the NFT back (Raffle.sol:329-337).
impact: The cohort of organic ticket holders who bought before the sale closed is left holding the loss.
  - k = 90,000: Alice's prize EV falls from 10,000 to 1,000 USDC (-9,000) for the same 10,000 USDC paid. S's EV rises from 9,500 to 14,000 (+4,500). The treasury takes +4,500 in fees on S's own entries.
  - EV-optimal k ≈ 34,721 (N + k = sqrt(20*V*N)): S gains about +6,028 and Alice loses about 7,764.
  - Under-subscribed raffle (Alice 100 entries, V = 10,000): S needs about 4,372 USDC of short-lived capital to cut Alice's prize EV from 10,000 to about 224 (S +9,558 EV).
mitigation: Stop the sale at the reserve in buyEntries (`if (lastEntry > reserveEntries) revert ...`), so no sponsor-rebated entries can be minted after organic demand meets the reserve. A buyer blocklist on sponsor/sponsorRecipient alone is not enough, because purchases are permissionless (sybil). A sponsor fill of the gap below the reserve remains possible; it is tracked as a separate lead.

fields.smell: The NftWon/CashWon regime check (Raffle.sol:521) counts sponsor-bought entries, which are rebated 95% through sponsorProceeds (Raffle.sol:544). When organic demand N < reserve R, the sponsor can fill R-N in the last block before endTime at a 5% cost. That turns a CashWon raffle (buyers' EV 0.8 USDC per entry) into NftWon. Example with R = 1,000, N = 900, NFT worth V = 500 USDC: honest CashWon gives buyers 720 USDC EV and the sponsor 135 USDC + the NFT (635). If the sponsor buys 100 entries, the raffle becomes NftWon: sponsor = 950 - 100 + 0.1*500 = 900 (+265); buyers' EV = 0.9*500 = 450 (-270); treasury +5.
fields.unverified: (1) Whether under-reserve buyers are entitled to expect CashWon. The reserve may be meant only as sponsor protection, and organic demand reaching R gives the same regime. (2) The flip pays only when V is below roughly 0.8*R (an overpriced reserve); with V = 900 in the example it is unprofitable and helps buyers. (3) There is no sybil-proof code fix: the sale cap proposed for the dilution FINDING does not close this gap.
fields.description: A sponsor-funded fill of the gap below the reserve in the last block lets the sponsor choose the payout regime after seeing demand, at a 5% cost, and moves EV from under-reserve buyers to the sponsor.

fields.smell: _update (Raffle.sol:497-502) allows ticket transfers in every status, including Drawing (the NatSpec at Raffle.sol:491 says so deliberately). The pending VRF fulfillment (wrapper -> rawFulfillRandomWords -> Raffle.sol:518) lets any mempool observer work out winningEntry before it executes. The observer can fill a stale marketplace listing of the winning ticket, or sell a losing ticket into a standing collection bid, ahead of or bundled right after the callback. Example: Alice lists ticket #7 (500 of 1,000 entries; NFT worth 2,000 USDC) at 900 USDC. Bob simulates the pending fulfillment, sees that entry 742 (in #7) wins, fills the listing first, and redeems the NFT. Alice's EV falls from about 1,000 to about 450.
fields.unverified: (1) Whether Chainlink's mainnet VRF fulfillments go through the public mempool. (2) Whether any fillable marketplace order exists at fulfillment time. (3) A Drawing-only transfer lock can be bypassed by bundling [fulfillment, fill], because status becomes NftWon mid-bundle. The only robust fix, blocking operator-initiated transfers from requestDraw onward, conflicts with the documented bearer-claim design. Victims are external order makers; the protocol's own accounting is unaffected.
fields.description: Tickets stay tradeable while the draw result can be derived publicly but is not yet on-chain, which allows trades against stale secondary-market orders by someone who already knows the result.

fields.smell: The outcome predicate `totalEntries >= reserveEntries` (Raffle.sol:521) counts the sponsor's own entries. In NftWon the sponsor gets back 95% of whatever it paid in (Raffle.sol:544). So the sponsor can meet its own reserve at about 5% cost and turn a CashWon (80% of the pot to a buyer) into an NftWon whenever the NFT is worth less than the cash prize. Worked example (arithmetic checked): reserve 1,000; buyers hold 900 entries; the NFT is worth 500 USDC. If the sponsor buys 100 entries before endTime, the sponsor's expected value rises by 265 USDC, the buyers' falls by 270 USDC and the treasury gains 5.
fields.unverified: Whether this is an accepted mechanism-design property. The reserve is public, any party can push the total over it, and the sponsor can buy from fresh addresses, so there is no on-chain fix.
fields.description: Buying the reserve shortfall with the sponsor's own money lets the sponsor pick the outcome branch that is worse for buyers. This is probably accepted design and is reported only for calibration.

fields.smell: DESIGN.md requires "Never move assets between raffle clones." `sponsorRecipient` is screened only at creation: `RaffleFactory._validateCreateParams` checks the `isRaffle` mapping (RaffleFactory.sol:163-169), and `Raffle.initialize` calls `_isProtocolDestination` (Raffle.sol:193), which skips the `isRaffle` query for addresses with no code (:602). Clones are deployed with CREATE (OZ `Clones.clone`: `create(value, 0x09, 0x37)`), so each future raffle address depends only on the factory address and nonce. These addresses can be predicted, and anyone can advance the nonce through the permissionless `createRaffle`. A sponsorRecipient equal to a future clone address therefore passes both screens. After a later `createRaffle` registers a raffle at that address, `releaseSponsorPrize` (:402-405) transfers the prize NFT into that clone without a delivery-time screen, and no function can ever move it out. The USDC path for the same recipient, `_transferQuote`, re-screens at payout (:565) and reverts, which strands `sponsorProceeds` instead. The same skip for code-less addresses in `_update` (:498 → :602) lets a ticket be sent to a future clone address, where it later becomes unreachable.

On current evidence this harms only the party who chose the address, so it is not reportable as a finding. It is listed because it is the one reachable state that violates DESIGN.md's cross-clone invariant, and because sibling payout sites screen inconsistently.

smell: DESIGN.md requires "Never move assets between raffle clones." `sponsorRecipient` is screened only at creation: `RaffleFactory._validateCreateParams` checks the `isRaffle` mapping (RaffleFactory.sol:163-169), and `Raffle.initialize` calls `_isProtocolDestination` (Raffle.sol:193), which skips the `isRaffle` query for addresses with no code (:602). Clones are deployed with CREATE (OZ `Clones.clone`: `create(value, 0x09, 0x37)`), so each future raffle address depends only on the factory address and nonce. These addresses can be predicted, and anyone can advance the nonce through the permissionless `createRaffle`. A sponsorRecipient equal to a future clone address therefore passes both screens. After a later `createRaffle` registers a raffle at that address, `releaseSponsorPrize` (:402-405) transfers the prize NFT into that clone without a delivery-time screen, and no function can ever move it out. The USDC path for the same recipient, `_transferQuote`, re-screens at payout (:565) and reverts, which strands `sponsorProceeds` instead. The same skip for code-less addresses in `_update` (:498 → :602) lets a ticket be sent to a future clone address, where it later becomes unreachable.
unverified: No actor other than the sponsor (for sponsorRecipient) or the ticket owner or operator (for tickets) chooses these destinations. Pointing at the raffle's own address is caught (:599, `destination == address(this)`), and a recipient that is already a raffle is caught (RaffleFactory.sol:166; Raffle.sol:602-603). On current evidence this harms only the party who chose the address, so it is not reportable as a finding. It is listed because it is the one reachable state that violates DESIGN.md's cross-clone invariant, and because sibling payout sites screen inconsistently.
description: Re-running `_isProtocolDestination(recipient, address(prizeToken))` before Raffle.sol:404 would make the NFT payout behave like `_transferQuote`, but because sponsorRecipient is immutable the prize would still be stranded rather than moved.

fields.smell: In NftWon, _settleWinningTicket makes 95% of the pot claimable by sponsorRecipient (Raffle.sol:544, :554). releaseSponsorProceeds (Raffle.sol:375-382) pays it without checking prizeClaimed or winnerRedeemed. The NFT leg (redeemWinningTicket, Raffle.sol:334-335) depends on the prize contract, which DESIGN.md says is untrusted, and it has no fallback: releaseSponsorPrize is barred in NftWon (Raffle.sol:397), and enableRefunds rejects terminal states (Raffle.sol:279-294). Suppose the prize contract permanently blocks transfers out of the clone (an admin pause, or a transfer-validator or blocklist entry on the clone address). Then the winning-ticket holder gets nothing while sponsorRecipient (950,000*T raw) and the treasury (50,000*T raw) are paid in full. Example with T = 10,000 entries: 9,500 USDC go to sponsorRecipient, 500 USDC go to the treasury, and the winning ticket is worthless.
fields.unverified: This is outside Lens 6 (no arithmetic defect). Unclear whether a sponsor can profit from it. Profit needs a prize contract where the sponsor controls an admin seizure or unfreeze path; otherwise it is only griefing. The IRaffle.sol NatSpec says "Supported prizes are honest, standards-compliant ERC-721s", which conflicts with DESIGN.md's untrusted-prize statement. Gating sponsor proceeds on prizeClaimed would create the opposite problem: proceeds held hostage by a winner who never redeems.
fields.description: The sponsor and treasury USDC legs settle independently of NFT delivery, so an undeliverable prize leaves only the winner unpaid, with no refund path.

fields.smell: The outcome test `totalEntries >= reserveEntries` (Raffle.sol:521) also counts entries the sponsor paid for. In NftWon, 95% of every entry, including the sponsor's own, returns to sponsorRecipient (Raffle.sol:544, :554). So the sponsor can flip a raffle that is below reserve from CashWon to NftWon for a 5% toll on the gap. Example: reserve 10,000 entries, 8,000 entries bought by other users. The sponsor buys 2,000 entries at endTime-1, which Raffle.sol:216 allows. Without the flip (CashWon), the winner gets 6,400 USDC and sponsorRecipient gets 1,200 USDC plus the NFT back. With the flip (NftWon), sponsorRecipient gets 9,500 USDC (net +7,500 after the 2,000 USDC outlay) and the sponsor's tickets have a 20% chance of winning the NFT. With the NFT worth 5,000 USDC: sponsor expected value rises from 6,200 to 8,500 (+2,300). The other buyers' expected value falls from 6,400 to 4,000 (-2,400). The treasury gains 100. The changes sum to zero.
fields.unverified: This is outside Lens 6 (economic/MEV). DESIGN.md does not forbid sponsor participation, and any address can buy (Sybil), so this may be an accepted property of reserve auctions. The flip only pays when the sponsor values the NFT below 0.8 x the pot from other buyers (here, below 7,875 USDC). Buyers can see totalEntries and reserveEntries on-chain, but they cannot exit before the outcome except by selling the ticket, because refundTickets requires Refunding.
fields.description: The sponsor can meet the reserve with their own entries, 95% of which come back to them, turning a cash raffle into an NFT raffle after buyers have committed.

fields.smell: Raffle.sol:544 sets the NftWon sponsor share to `grossPot - protocolFee`. grossPot (L539) includes every purchase, whoever made it. Nothing in buyEntries (L209-237) or _update (L497-502) excludes the sponsor or sponsorRecipient as buyer or recipient. So under NftWon an entry the sponsor buys from any address nets out at 1,000,000 - 950,000 = 50,000 raw units (0.05 USDC), while every other buyer pays 1 USDC. Sales close at endTime (L216), so nobody can respond to a buy in the last block before it.
fields.unverified: Whether the design accepts sponsor participation. DESIGN.md does not forbid it, and the money map lists "may also buy entries" as a normal sponsor action. No identity check survives Sybil addresses, so there is no single small code fix. A design change such as capping the NftWon sponsor share at reserveEntries*ENTRY_PRICE, with the excess paid to the winner, fixes (a) but not (b). The losses are expected-value transfers, not deterministic theft.
fields.description: Because L544 rebates 95% of the sponsor's own spend, a last-block dilution or reserve flip has positive expected value for the sponsor. Non-sponsor buyers carry the loss, and the treasury captures part of it.

fields.smell: Tickets stay transferable while status == Drawing and within the block that resolves the draw. _update (L497-502) only rejects protocol addresses (L599-604), and L491 says this is intended. On Ethereum L1 the Chainlink fulfillment transaction carries the VRF proof in the public mempool. A searcher can compute randomWords[0] % totalEntries + 1 (L518) and map it to a ticket with ticketRange (L451-455) before L521 executes.
fields.unverified: That holders actually leave marketplace orders open across requestDraw. That the VRF node broadcasts publicly rather than through a private relay. Freezing transfers only during Drawing does not stop a same-block back-run of the fulfillment. The fix is therefore a design choice: block transfers other than mint and burn from requestDraw until block.timestamp > resolvedAt, and document that holders must cancel orders before the draw.
fields.description: Because bearer tickets can be traded across a public randomness reveal, any searcher can snipe stale listings. The victims are ticket holders with open orders; the protocol's own accounting is unaffected.

fields.smell: NftWon is a terminal state with no exit if the prize leg can never complete. In NftWon the NFT can only leave through prizeToken.transferFrom(address(this), winner, id) plus the ownerOf re-check (Raffle.sol:334-337). releaseSponsorPrize rejects NftWon (Raffle.sol:397-399). enableRefunds rejects every terminal status (Raffle.sol:279-293). No path turns an undeliverable prize into refunds or cash. Settlement, however, has already credited sponsorProceeds = grossPot - protocolFee (Raffle.sol:544, 554), and releaseSponsorProceeds pays it without checking prizeClaimed (Raffle.sol:375-382). Path: (1) sponsor S escrows token #1 of collection P via createRaffle with reserveEntries = 1,000; (2) buyers buy 1,000 entries = 1,000 USDC; (3) the VRF callback resolves NftWon (Raffle.sol:521); (4) anyone settles: sponsorProceeds = 950 USDC, protocolFees = 50 USDC; (5) anyone calls releaseSponsorProceeds and 950 USDC goes to sponsorRecipient; (6) P permanently blocks transfers out of the clone (admin pause, per-address blocklist, a transfer-validator policy that turns off owner-initiated transfers by contracts, or a sponsor-controlled P whose transferFrom reverts or whose ownerOf lies); (7) every redeemWinningTicket call reverts, which undoes the burn (Raffle.sol:325, 334-337). The winning ticket cannot be refunded either (Raffle.sol:350). Outcome: all 1,000 USDC from buyers is paid out (950 to the sponsor, 50 to the treasury). The winning-ticket holder keeps a claim that can never be redeemed, and the NFT is stuck in the clone with no recovery path.
fields.unverified: (a) Whether the trust model makes this reportable. DESIGN.md says arbitrary prize contracts are untrusted, but it also says "Sponsor and treasury can claim independently after settlement", and IRaffle.sol:14-15 limits support to "honest, standards-compliant ERC-721s". (b) Whether blocking delivery adds any loss. If the sponsor controls P, blocking adds nothing over raffling a worthless token: the sponsor collects 950 either way. A sponsor also gains nothing by blocking a valuable token, because it is stuck for them too. Extra loss only appears when a third-party admin of a real collection permanently restricts transfers out of the clone. Working offline, I could not confirm any live collection that accepts the factory's inbound safeTransferFrom (RaffleFactory.sol:128) but later blocks the raffle's outbound transferFrom. (c) A temporary pause only delays the winner: there is no redemption deadline, so they can redeem after the unpause.
fields.description: The NftWon branch ties a final state to a delivery made by an untrusted contract while paying the sponsor's 95% with no condition. The smallest code fix is to make releaseSponsorProceeds (Raffle.sol:375-382) require prizeClaimed when status == NftWon, or to add a fallback for failed delivery. Both conflict with DESIGN.md's "claim independently after settlement", and the first lets a winner who never redeems freeze the sponsor's share.

fields.smell: The VRF wrapper can never change. RaffleFactory stores it as an immutable (RaffleFactory.sol:86), builds it into the single implementation (RaffleFactory.sol:89, inherited immutable i_vrfV2PlusWrapper), has no admin to repoint it, and createRaffle (RaffleFactory.sol:97-148) never checks that the wrapper still works. If the wrapper is disabled or unconfigured, getVrfRequestPrice and requestRandomnessPayInNative (Raffle.sol:249, 257) revert for every raffle. If the wrapper's subscription runs out of funds, a paid request is accepted but never fulfilled. After such an event, sponsors can still create raffles and buyers can still buy (Raffle.sol:209-237), but no raffle can ever resolve. Each one only moves to Refunding at endTime + 2d (Raffle.sol:286-287) or drawRequestedAt + 2d (Raffle.sol:290-291). Buyers' USDC and sponsors' NFTs are locked for up to 30d of sale + 2d (or + 4d). In the unfunded case, whoever requests the draw loses the native VRF fee.
fields.unverified: The wrapper implementation is not in node_modules; only VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase.sol and IVRFV2PlusWrapper.sol are. The disabled and unfunded behaviour therefore comes from public Chainlink v2.5 semantics, not from source in the repo. No principal is lost because the refund path stays intact. DESIGN.md treats the wrapper as a trusted canonical dependency and rules out mutable configuration, so this is probably accepted design. The impact is limited to time-bounded locking.
fields.description: Because the wrapper is immutable and never checked, a deprecation on Chainlink's side puts every live and future raffle into a "lock, then refund" mode that only redeploying the factory can fix.

fields.smell: (Outside the DoS lens; passed on.) Tickets stay transferable while status == Drawing. Raffle.sol:497-502 only screens destinations, and Raffle.sol:491 says tickets are transferable "in every lifecycle state". So the input that decides who gets paid, ticket ownership, can change after the VRF request. The calldata of the coordinator's fulfillment fixes randomWords[0]. Anyone watching the mempool can therefore compute winningEntry = randomWords[0] % totalEntries + 1 (Raffle.sol:518) and the ticket that contains it before the callback lands. They can then trade ahead of it: buy the winning ticket from an open listing, or sell known losing tickets into open collection offers. Path: a CashWon raffle with 1,000 entries and a 1,000 USDC pot. Holder H has an open listing for ticket #7 (entries 101-110) at 9 USDC. The fulfillment transaction is pending, and its random word maps to entry 105. A bot fills H's listing at 9 USDC before the callback, then calls redeemWinningTicket(7) after resolution and receives 800 USDC (Raffle.sol:339-342). H gives up about 791 USDC of value.
fields.unverified: I could not confirm offline whether Ethereum-mainnet VRF fulfillments go through the public mempool. Even if they do not, a back-run right after resolution sniping a stale listing causes the same loss to the seller. fields.smell: USDC payouts re-screen the recipient at payout time through _transferQuote (Raffle.sol:564-567). The two NFT payouts, releaseSponsorPrize (Raffle.sol:404) and redeemWinningTicket NftWon (Raffle.sol:334), do not. Two earlier screens both accept a not-yet-deployed CREATE address of the factory's next clone as sponsorRecipient: the init-time screen (Raffle.sol:193 via _isProtocolDestination, which skips the registry for code-less addresses at :602) and the factory screen (F:166, isRaffle mapping). Once a clone is created at that address, anyone can call releaseSponsorPrize and push the prize into another raffle clone. That breaks DESIGN.md "Never move assets between raffle clones", and the NFT cannot be recovered there (no rescue path, Raffle.sol:410-411). releaseSponsorProceeds meanwhile reverts with InvalidQuoteDestination forever.

fields.root_cause: Raffle.sol:376. `releaseSponsorProceeds` pays out `sponsorProceeds` with no check on `status` or `prizeClaimed`. In `NftWon`, `_settleWinningTicket` allocates 95% to the sponsor and 5% to the treasury (Raffle.sol:543-544, 554-555) through permissionless, storage-only settlement. Neither step depends on the NFT leg in `redeemWinningTicket` (Raffle.sol:329-337) ever succeeding. `NftWon` also has no fallback for the winner: `enableRefunds` only accepts Active or Drawing (Raffle.sol:279-293), `releaseSponsorPrize` excludes NftWon (Raffle.sol:397), and `winnerProceeds` stays 0. The code assumes the escrowed ERC-721 can still be transferred out of the clone when the winner redeems. Real ERC-721s let an admin revoke that after deposit: OpenZeppelin `ERC721Pausable` (`_update` is `whenNotPaused` and reverts `EnforcedPause()`), Manifold Creator Core's admin-set transfer-approval hook (`setApproveTransfer`), Limit Break ERC721-C transfer validators (creator-set soulbound or OTC-blocking policies, account freezing), and upgradeable ERC-721 proxies. DESIGN.md says "arbitrary prize contracts ... are untrusted", but IRaffle.sol:14-15 assumes "honest" prizes. The code follows the weaker of the two.
fields.internal_pre: The reserve is met, so the result is `NftWon`. No other state is needed.
fields.external_pre: The prize collection has an owner-controlled transfer gate (pause, approve-transfer hook, validator policy or freeze, or proxy upgrade), and the sponsor controls it or colludes with whoever does. The common case qualifies: an artist raffling a token from their own Manifold or OpenZeppelin collection.
fields.impact: The buyer cohort paid 20,000 USDC. S takes 19,000 USDC and the treasury 1,000 USDC, and the NFT is never delivered. Winner W is left holding the loss: the claim on C#7 can never be redeemed and there is no cash or refund substitute. This defeats the protocol's trust-minimising guarantee ("Exactly one ERC721 prize is escrowed atomically at creation") while fully protecting the sponsor's 95%. S's cost is a token S controls anyway.
fields.mitigation: In `releaseSponsorProceeds` (Raffle.sol:375-376), add `if (status == Status.NftWon && !prizeClaimed) revert` so NftWon sponsor proceeds unlock only after `redeemWinningTicket` has delivered and verified the prize. Optionally apply the same gate to `releaseProtocolFees`. This narrows DESIGN.md's "claim independently after settlement" for the NftWon branch only. That is the branch where the sponsor can control the opposite leg, and the gate removes the sponsor's profit from blocking the prize.

  1. Artist S owns collection C, an OZ v5 `ERC721` + `ERC721Pausable` + `Ownable` contract that reports `supportsInterface(0x80ac58cd) == true`. C is unpaused and S holds C#7.
  2. S calls `RaffleFactory.createRaffle({sponsorRecipient: S, prizeToken: C, prizeTokenId: 7, reserveEntries: 1_000, endTime: now + 7 days})`. The escrow at F:128-134 succeeds and raffle R is Active, holding C#7.
  3. Buyers purchase 20,000 entries. R now holds 20,000 USDC and `unsettledPot = 20_000e6`.
  4. After `endTime`, S already knows the result will be `NftWon` (20,000 >= 1,000 is fixed before randomness), so S calls `C.pause()`. No draw or refund path touches C. With a per-address gate (a Manifold hook rejecting `from == R`, or an ERC721-C freeze of R), S's other collectors are not affected.
  5. S calls `R.requestDraw{value: fee}()`. The VRF callback sets `status = NftWon` and `winningEntry = 13_337`, which falls in buyer W's ticket #412.
  6. S calls `R.settleWinningTicket(412)`, which is permissionless and makes no NFT check. Result: `sponsorProceeds = 19_000e6`, `protocolFees = 1_000e6`.
  7. S calls `R.releaseSponsorProceeds()` and receives 19,000 USDC. Anyone calls `releaseProtocolFees()` and the treasury receives 1,000 USDC.
  8. W calls `R.redeemWinningTicket(412)`. `C.transferFrom(R, W, 7)` reverts `EnforcedPause()`, so the whole call reverts and the ticket is not burned. Every retry reverts for as long as C stays gated, and no other claim path exists in `NftWon`. Upgradeable variant: S upgrades C, pulls C#7 back out of R, and still keeps the 19,000 USDC.

fields.unverified: Whether sponsor-controlled or admin-mutable prize contracts are in the threat model. DESIGN.md says "arbitrary prize contracts ... are untrusted", but IRaffle.sol:14-15 says "Supported prizes are honest, standards-compliant ERC-721s". DESIGN.md also says "Sponsor and treasury can claim independently after settlement", so the independence is deliberate. Any delivery gate must still handle a winner who never redeems, because there is no redemption deadline. A fully malicious prize can fake both escrow and delivery, so no on-chain change protects against it. The gap is concrete only for admin-mutable collections (upgradeable, pausable or blocklisting).
